claims.text: Lattice distortion in HEA protective coatings arises from high configurational entropy.
The degree of lattice distortion is the dominant microstructural mediator governing wear resistance in HEA protective coatings.
Lattice distortion enhances wear resistance by impeding localized plastic deformation during wear.
The baseline coatings are fully dense and microstructurally homogeneous.
A nominal equiatomic composition yields maximum lattice distortion.
Slight compositional adjustment that reduces atomic-radius mismatch will systematically reduce overall lattice distortion while retaining high-entropy conditions.
Lattice distortion governs solid-solution strengthening in the coatings.
Solid-solution strengthening controls deformation behavior under wear conditions.
Lattice distortion raises barriers to dislocation motion.
Raised barriers to dislocation motion suppress localized plastic deformation.
Reducing lattice distortion makes wear-induced deformation easier and consequently lowers wear resistance.
Compositionally modified coatings with reduced lattice distortion will have higher wear rates than baseline equiatomic coatings.
Compositionally modified coatings with reduced lattice distortion will exhibit more pronounced plastic deformation than baseline equiatomic coatings.
The proposed effect applies over a moderate-temperature range in which diffusion is not dominant.
The proposed effect applies while high mixing entropy is maintained and secondary phases are absent.
Large deviations from high-entropy conditions or the introduction of secondary phases may activate other wear mechanisms.
Grain size may affect the measured relationship between lattice distortion and wear.
Protective oxide-layer formation may also contribute to wear performance.
